title: The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus
subject: litterature
description: Camus starts from suicide to define the absurd. Sisyphus, condemned to roll a rock, becomes the hero of lucid joy.

hero.hook: A single truly serious philosophical problem, writes Camus. Then he responds differently than expected.

blocks.text: **The Myth of Sisyphus**, published in **1942**, is the founding essay of the thought of the absurd at **Albert Camus**. Written in the middle of **Second World War**, he seeks how to live without consoling illusions: neither religious faith, nor political utopias.

Camus relies on **Sisyphus**, king of Corinth condemned by the gods to useless and endless work, to transform despair into an ethic of freedom. The essay accompanies the novel **The Stranger** in the cycle of the absurd.

sections.title: The divorce between man and the world

blocks.text: Camus opens with: “There is only one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide. » Judging whether life is worth living is the fundamental question. Any reflection on meaning starts from there.

blocks.caption: Camus in the 1940s: lucidity in the face of the absurd.

blocks.text: Camus considered including an appendix on Kafka, removed by the censor. He almost titled his manuscript “The Absurd”.

The absurd is neither in the world nor in man alone, but in their confrontation: the mind aspires to order and meaning, the world remains silent. Recognizing the absurd is the first step towards intellectual honesty, before any response. Camus refuses false escapes, whether they come from religion or politics.

Camus identifies three responses to the absurd. Physical suicide removes the witness of the absurd: it is a logical error, an escape. Philosophical suicide, or , refuge in faith or the irrational, flees the problem instead of confronting it. **[[The philosophical "leap" (Kierkegaard)]]**

The only authentic response is : standing in the face of the silence of the world, maintaining tension without consolation. The absurd man lives in the present, without metaphysical hope placed in a beyond or an end of history. **[[The absurd revolt]]**

sections.title: You have to imagine Sisyphus happy

blocks.text: **Sisyphus**, in Greek mythology, cheated death. Punishment: he must roll a rock eternally to the top of a mountain, from where it always comes back down. Camus is interested in the moment of descent: Sisyphus is then superior to his destiny because he is conscious.

blocks.caption: Sisyphus and his rock: useless effort becoming inner victory.

blocks.text: You have to imagine Sisyphus happy.
blocks.attribution: Albert Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus

blocks.text: This happiness is not naive: it is the victory of a man who knows that his pain will have no end, and who accepts the struggle as a filling of the heart. Happiness and the absurd are born from the same earth. Camus refuses despair as he refuses illusion.

sections.title: From the absurd to the revolt

blocks.text: The essay offers an alternative to the existentialism of **Jean-Paul Sartre**, a philosophy centered on freedom and responsibility. Camus offers a freedom celebrating the moment. It influences the  of **Samuel Beckett** and **Eugène Ionesco**, where the characters go around in a loop without finding meaning. **[[Theater of the absurd]]**

events.title: The Rebel Man
events.detail: Camus opens the cycle of social revolt.

blocks.text: Camus does not deny pain. He refuses to transform it into dogma. Sisyphus goes back down the slope knowing what he is doing: this is what makes destiny, sometimes, habitable. The essay remains an essential reading companion for **The Stranger**. He also analyzes writers of the absurd, from **Dostoyevsky** to **Kafka**, to show how art expresses the human condition.
**The Myth of Sisyphus**, published in **1942**, transforms the absurd into : remaining lucid, refusing illusions, and imagining Sisyphus happy in his endless struggle. **[[The absurd revolt]]**
